scope_note: Free public programs, nonprofits and official locators for families raising children and young adults with autism, ADHD, developmental, learning, physical, medical or behavioral health disabilities. Private therapy providers are not listed. Contacts come from published official or organization sources and are not telephone-confirmed.

resources.name: CDC milestone checklists and Milestone Tracker app
resources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.what: Free checklists for ages 2 months to 5 years, in English and Spanish, to track how your child plays, learns, speaks, acts and moves.
resources.how: Fill out the checklist for your child's age and bring it to the next doctor visit. You do not need to wait for a diagnosis to ask for an evaluation.

resources.name: Find your state's early intervention program
resources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.what: Every state runs a free early intervention program for children under 3 with delays or disabilities. Parents can call directly. No doctor's referral is needed.
resources.how: Look up your state's contact and ask for a free evaluation. If your child is 3 or older, call your local public school district instead, even if your child does not attend that school.

resources.name: Your state's Parent Training and Information Center
resources.org: Center for Parent Information and Resources
resources.what: Every state has at least one free, federally funded parent center for families of children with any disability, birth to 26. Staff help with IEPs, 504 plans, school meetings and your rights.
resources.how: Choose your state on the map to find its parent center, then call before your next school meeting.

resources.name: Family-to-Family Health Information Center
resources.what: Family-led centers in every state help parents of children with special health care needs work with doctors, insurance, Medicaid and disability services.
resources.how: Choose your state to find its family-to-family center or Family Voices affiliate.

resources.name: Autism Society National Helpline
resources.what: Information and referral specialists help families find local autism services, affiliates and support groups. It is not a crisis line.
resources.how: Call or use the online form. Ask about the Autism Society affiliate in your state.

resources.name: National Resource Center on ADHD helpline
resources.what: Health information specialists answer questions about ADHD diagnosis, treatment, school supports and finding local help. Spanish-speaking specialists are available.
resources.how: Call the ADHD helpline or use the website's parent toolkits and local support-group finder.

resources.name: SSI for children with disabilities
resources.what: Monthly payments for children with qualifying disabilities in families with limited income and resources. In most states, SSI also opens the door to Medicaid. Benefits are reviewed again at age 18 under adult rules.
resources.how: Start online or call to set up an appointment. Have your child's medical and school records ready.

resources.name: National Respite Locator
resources.what: Find respite programs, short breaks for family caregivers, and ways to pay for them in your state.
resources.how: Search by state and the kind of care your child needs. Listings are not complete, so also ask your county or state disability agency.

resources.name: Help Me Grow Early Intervention
resources.org: Ohio Department of Children and Youth
resources.what: Ohio's free early intervention program for children under 3 with delays or disabilities, available in all 88 counties. Services usually happen at home. Anyone can refer, and parents can refer themselves.
resources.how: Call or complete the online referral. A local coordinator contacts the family. If your child is close to 3, call right away, because early intervention ends at the third birthday and the school district takes over.

resources.name: Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD)
resources.org: Ohio's Parent Training and Information Center
resources.what: Free help for Ohio families of children with any disability, birth through 26: understanding evaluations, IEPs, rights and school meetings. Based in Marion.
resources.how: Call before an evaluation or IEP meeting, or when you disagree with the school.

resources.name: Ohio Parent Mentors
resources.what: Parent mentors are parents of children with disabilities who work with school districts and educational service centers to help other families through special education.
resources.how: Ask your school district or educational service center whether a parent mentor serves your area.

resources.name: Ohio special education: information for families
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: The state's guide for families of students with disabilities, including evaluations, IEPs, parent rights and where to get help.
resources.how: To ask for a free evaluation, write to your school district's special education director. Keep a copy and note the date you sent it.

resources.name: Autism Scholarship Program
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Pays for special education services from approved private providers or other public programs for children identified with autism who have an IEP from their school district.
resources.how: Read the parent information, then confirm your child's IEP and autism identification with your district before you apply.

resources.name: Jon Peterson Special Needs Scholarship
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Pays for special education services from approved providers for children with an IEP. The maximum amount depends on the child's disability category.
resources.how: Visit the program page or email peterson.scholarship@education.ohio.gov with questions.

resources.name: OCALI (Ohio Center for Autism and Low Incidence)
resources.org: Funded by the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Guides, training and a family outreach center for families of children with autism and low-incidence disabilities, from early childhood into adulthood.
resources.how: Start with the family section of the website for guides and the lending library.

resources.name: Your county board of developmental disabilities
resources.what: Your county board is the local starting point for developmental disability services: eligibility, service coordination, Medicaid waivers, family support funds and, in some counties, early intervention.
resources.how: Find your county's board on the directory map, or call the Ohio Department of Developmental Disabilities to be referred to your county.

resources.name: Ohio Medicaid for children
resources.what: Health coverage for children in eligible families, including checkups, therapies and behavioral health services. Children with disabilities may also qualify through SSI or a county board waiver.
resources.how: Apply online at benefits.ohio.gov, by phone or at your county Department of Job and Family Services.

resources.name: OhioRISE
resources.org: Ohio Department of Medicaid with Aetna Better Health of Ohio
resources.what: A specialized Medicaid program for children and youth 0–20 with significant behavioral health needs. It adds care coordination, in-home and crisis services.
resources.how: Ask your child's Medicaid plan, doctor or behavioral health provider about a CANS assessment for OhioRISE.

resources.name: Complex Medical Help (formerly Children with Medical Handicaps)
resources.what: Helps pay for diagnosis and treatment of eligible chronic medical conditions and links families to approved providers. The diagnostic program can help confirm a diagnosis.
resources.how: Contact the public health nurse at your county or city health department to start the application.

resources.name: STABLE Account (Ohio's ABLE account)
resources.what: A tax-advantaged savings account for people with disabilities that does not count against SSI or Medicaid limits in the way an ordinary savings account would.
resources.how: Read the program details or call the STABLE team before opening an account.

resources.name: Pre-Employment Transition Services
resources.what: Free job exploration, work-based learning, workplace readiness, self-advocacy and college counseling for students with disabilities, starting at age 14.
resources.how: Ask your child's IEP team or school transition coordinator to request Pre-ETS from OOD.

resources.name: Resolving special education disagreements
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Ohio's guidance on settling special education disputes early: talk with the district's special education director, ask a parent mentor or parent center for help, and use facilitated meetings or mediation.
resources.how: Read the information sheet before you escalate, and keep written records of every request.

resources.name: Military OneSource special needs consultations
resources.what: Free consultants help military families with special education, TRICARE, EFMP and community services. Retirees and honorably discharged service members can use Military OneSource for 365 days after separation.
resources.how: Call 24/7 or start a secure chat to schedule a phone or video consultation.

resources.name: Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP)
resources.what: Active duty families enroll a family member with special medical or educational needs so assignments and family support take those needs into account. EFMP enrollment is also required for some TRICARE programs.
resources.how: Contact your installation's EFMP family support office or Military OneSource.

resources.name: TRICARE Extended Care Health Option (ECHO)
resources.what: Extra benefits for eligible active duty family members with qualifying disabilities: training, special education, assistive technology, home health care and respite care for the primary caregiver.
resources.how: Contact your TRICARE regional contractor to register. Services need pre-authorization.

resources.name: TRICARE Autism Care Demonstration
resources.what: TRICARE's route to applied behavior analysis (ABA) for beneficiaries diagnosed with autism, with no yearly or lifetime cap. Active duty families also need EFMP enrollment (unless waived) and ECHO registration.
resources.how: Follow the enrollment steps on the TRICARE page and work with the assigned autism services navigator.

resources.name: STOMP: Specialized Training of Military Parents
resources.what: The parent training and information center for military families of children with disabilities, in the U.S. or overseas. Workshops and webinars are open to all military-connected families.
resources.how: Call or check upcoming virtual workshops.

resources.name: CHAMPVA health coverage for veterans' children
resources.what: Health coverage for children of veterans rated permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected disability (or who died from one), when the family is not eligible for TRICARE. Coverage usually ends at 18, or 23 for full-time students, but a child who became permanently unable to support themselves before 18 may stay eligible.
resources.how: Check eligibility and apply on VA.gov, or ask a county veterans service officer to help with the paperwork.

changes.title: Federal special education oversight is moving
changes.text: In June 2026 the U.S. Department of Education announced agreements moving day-to-day administration of special education programs to the Department of Health and Human Services and civil rights enforcement to the Department of Justice. The law itself, including your child's right to a free appropriate public education and an IEP, has not changed. Your school district and state remain responsible for services.

changes.title: TRICARE autism coverage is under review
changes.text: A National Academies study recommended replacing the Autism Care Demonstration with ABA as a regular TRICARE benefit, and senators have urged the Defense Department to act on it. Check TRICARE's page for the current rules before you enroll.
